title: Orienting Yourself: The Use of Coordinates

learn.hook: Long before GPS, Indian astronomers were already giving addresses to stars!
points: A coordinate system is a framework that fixes the exact location of a place or point using numbers.
Cities of the Sindhu-Sarasvati civilisation, such as Mohenjo-daro and Dholavira, had streets laid out in a grid, mostly meeting at right angles.
Indian astronomers used Ujjayini (Ujjain) as a reference line for longitude, and Aryabhata described positions of heavenly bodies with angle-like coordinates.
Brahmagupta gave rules for working with zero and negative numbers; Al-Biruni located cities using latitude and longitude; Omar Khayyam solved algebra problems with geometry.
René Descartes showed that any point on a flat surface can be named by just two numbers, joining algebra and geometry. That is why the plane is called Cartesian.

example.q: Why are negative numbers (made popular in India by Brahmagupta's rules) needed for a coordinate system with the origin in the middle?
steps: Places to the left of or below the origin must also get numbers.
Positive numbers alone can only describe one side of each axis.
Negative numbers name the other side.
example.answer: They let us name points on both sides of the origin.

learn.reallife: A railway ticket's seat number (coach S4, berth 23) is a simple two-number coordinate system that tells you exactly where to sit.

topics.title: Making a floor map to scale

learn.hook: How do you fit a whole room onto one sheet of paper? Shrink it with a scale!
points: A floor map shows a room as seen from above, with each object drawn in its place.
A tactile map is one you read by touch: pins can mark corners of objects and threads can show the walls, so a person who cannot see can feel the layout.
A scale links paper and real sizes, for example 1 cm on paper = 1 foot in the room. Multiply paper length by the scale to get the real length.
Only things standing on the floor (bed, table, door) can be marked on a floor map. A window or ceiling fan is above the floor, so it has no spot on the floor plan.

example.q: A room is 12 feet long and 9 feet wide. Using 1 cm = 1 foot, what size should the map be? Using 1 cm = 3 feet?

learn.reallife: School fire-exit plans pasted near classroom doors are floor maps drawn to scale.

quiz.q: Which item belongs on a floor map of a classroom?

Decide what can appear on a floor map.
Know what a tactile map is and how it is made.

Tactile map: pins for corners, threads for walls and edges.

Windows and ceiling fans are not on a floor map.

learn.hook: How do you tell a friend exactly where your seat is in a cinema hall? Row and seat number! Two numbers can pin down any spot.
points: Two perpendicular number lines make the Cartesian plane: the horizontal x-axis and the vertical y-axis.
The axes meet at the origin O, whose coordinates are (0, 0).
Every point is named by an ordered pair (x, y). The x-coordinate (abscissa) tells how far left or right; the y-coordinate (ordinate) tells how far up or down.
Order matters: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points.
A point on the x-axis has y = 0, and a point on the y-axis has x = 0.

example.q: Point P is 4 units to the right of the y-axis and 3 units below the x-axis. Write its coordinates.
steps: Right of the y-axis means x is positive: x = 4
Below the x-axis means y is negative: y = −3

learn.reallife: Maps on your phone use latitude and longitude, which is a coordinate system on the Earth. Chess squares like e4 work the same way.

games.title: True or false?
items: (3, 7) and (7, 3) are the same point
Order matters: the first number is x and the second is y, so these are two different points.
Every point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0
On the y-axis you have not moved left or right at all, so x = 0.
The point (0, −4) lies on the x-axis
Its x-coordinate is 0, so it lies on the y-axis, 4 units below the origin.
The x-axis and the y-axis are perpendicular to each other
The two axes cross at a right angle at the origin.
The ordinate of (6, −1) is 6
The ordinate is the y-coordinate, which is −1.

quiz.q: In the point (−6, 2), what is the abscissa?
quiz.explain: The abscissa is the x-coordinate, the first number of the ordered pair.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up abscissa (x) and ordinate (y), or drops the negative sign

quiz.q: What is the ordinate of the point (5, −9)?
quiz.explain: The ordinate is the y-coordinate, the second number of the pair.
quiz.mistake: Thinks the ordinate is the first number, or ignores the sign

quiz.q: Which point lies on the y-axis?
quiz.explain: Points on the y-axis have x-coordinate 0, so (0, 7) is on the y-axis, 7 units above the origin.
steps: A point on the y-axis has x-coordinate 0.
(7, 0) has y = 0, so it is on the x-axis.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a 0 in the y place puts the point on the y-axis

quiz.q: Where do the x-axis and the y-axis meet?
quiz.explain: The two axes cross at the origin, where both coordinates are zero.
steps: The x-axis and y-axis are perpendicular number lines.
They cross at the origin O, where x = 0 and y = 0.
quiz.mistake: Thinks counting starts at 1 on the axes

quiz.q: Arjun stands at the origin, walks 3 units left and then 5 units up. What are his coordinates now?
quiz.explain: Left makes x negative, so x = −3. Up makes y positive, so y = 5. He is at (−3, 5).
quiz.mistake: Forgets that moving left gives a negative x-coordinate

quiz.q: Point A is at (4, 0). How far is A from the origin?
quiz.explain: A is on the x-axis, 4 steps to the right of the origin.
steps: A lies on the x-axis because y = 0
quiz.mistake: Reads the 0 as the distance

quiz.q: Which statement about the point (2, 9) is correct?
options: It is 2 units from the x-axis and 9 units from the y-axis
It is 2 units from the y-axis and 9 units from the x-axis
quiz.explain: The x-coordinate 2 tells how far the point is from the y-axis; the y-coordinate 9 tells how far it is from the x-axis.
steps: In (x, y), x tells the distance from the y-axis; y tells the distance from the x-axis.
For (2, 9): 2 units from the y-axis, 9 units from the x-axis.
Neither coordinate is 0, so it is on no axis.
Answer: It is 2 units from the y-axis and 9 units from the x-axis
quiz.mistake: Matches the x-coordinate with the x-axis distance instead of the y-axis distance

quiz.q: How far is the point (−5, 3) from the y-axis?
quiz.explain: Distance from the y-axis is the size of the x-coordinate. A distance is never negative, so it is 5 units.
quiz.mistake: Uses the y-coordinate, or gives a negative distance

teach.ask: Gappu tilts his head: "Why do you need TWO numbers to name a point? Isn't one number enough?"
teach.praise: Chirp! One number for across, one for up or down, and the order matters. Now I can find any spot!
teach.nudge: But which number do I use first, the across one or the up one?

revise.summary: The Cartesian plane is made by two perpendicular number lines, the x-axis and y-axis, meeting at the origin (0, 0). Every point is an ordered pair (x, y).
focus: Write the coordinates of a point from its position.
Know abscissa and ordinate.
Spot points on the axes.
remember: Origin O = (0, 0).
x-coordinate = abscissa (left/right); y-coordinate = ordinate (up/down).
On the x-axis y = 0; on the y-axis x = 0.
4 right of the y-axis and 3 below the x-axis: (4, −3).
traps: (2, 5) and (5, 2) are different points: order matters.
A 0 in the y place puts the point on the x-axis, not the y-axis.
x tells the distance from the y-axis, not from the x-axis.

learn.hook: The two axes cut the plane like a roti cut into four pieces. Each piece has its own sign pattern!
points: The axes divide the plane into four quadrants, numbered I, II, III, IV going anticlockwise from the top right.
Signs of (x, y): Quadrant I (+, +), Quadrant II (−, +), Quadrant III (−, −), Quadrant IV (+, −).
A point on an axis does not belong to any quadrant.
Distance between two points: across distance and up distance form the two shorter sides of a right triangle, so by Pythagoras, distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
Distance of (x, y) from the origin = √(x² + y²).

example.q: Find the distance between A(1, 2) and B(4, 6).

learn.reallife: Delivery apps estimate the straight-line distance between your home and a shop using coordinates and this very formula.

quiz.q: In which quadrant does (−5, 8) lie?
quiz.explain: x is negative and y is positive: (−, +) is Quadrant II, the top-left part.
steps: (−5, 8): x is negative, y is positive.
quiz.mistake: Numbers the quadrants clockwise instead of anticlockwise

quiz.q: A point has a negative x-coordinate and a negative y-coordinate. Which quadrant is it in?
quiz.explain: (−, −) means left of the y-axis and below the x-axis: the bottom-left part, Quadrant III.
steps: Negative x and negative y: sign pattern (−, −).
(−, −) is Quadrant III, the bottom-left part.
quiz.mistake: Confuses Quadrant III with Quadrant IV

quiz.q: Which point is in Quadrant IV?
quiz.explain: Quadrant IV has positive x and negative y. Only (3, −2) has the sign pattern (+, −).
steps: (−3, 2) is II, (−3, −2) is III, (0, −2) is on the y-axis.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a point on an axis such as (0, −2) belongs to a quadrant

quiz.q: Where does the point (0, −6) lie?
options: On the y-axis, in no quadrant
quiz.explain: Its x-coordinate is 0, so it sits on the y-axis. Points on the axes are not in any quadrant.
steps: So it lies on the y-axis.
Points on an axis belong to no quadrant.
Answer: On the y-axis, in no quadrant
quiz.mistake: Assigns a quadrant to a point that lies on an axis

quiz.q: Find the distance between A(2, 1) and B(8, 9).
quiz.explain: Across 6 and up 8 form the legs of a right triangle; the distance is the hypotenuse.
quiz.mistake: Adds 6 and 8 instead of using Pythagoras, or forgets the square root

quiz.q: How far is the point (−5, −12) from the origin?
quiz.explain: Use √(x² + y²). Squaring removes the negative signs.
quiz.mistake: Adds the coordinates directly instead of squaring them

quiz.q: On a town map (1 unit = 1 km), Harpreet's house is at (−3, 4) and her school is at (5, 4). What is the straight distance between them?
quiz.explain: Both points have y = 4, so the line joining them is horizontal. Subtract the x-coordinates.
quiz.mistake: Computes 5 − 3 = 2, forgetting that subtracting a negative means adding

quiz.q: The point (a, 3) lies in Quadrant II. Which value can a be?
quiz.explain: Quadrant II needs a negative x-coordinate. Only −4 is negative. (a = 0 would put the point on the y-axis.)
steps: Quadrant II needs x negative and y positive.
y = 3 is positive, so a must be negative.
a = 0 would put the point on the y-axis. Only −4 is negative.
quiz.mistake: Forgets that Quadrant II has negative x-values

teach.ask: Gappu scratches his feathers: "How can I tell which quadrant a point is in without drawing it?"
teach.praise: Just look at the signs of x and y! (+, +) is I, then go anticlockwise. Easy peasy!
teach.nudge: Do the signs of x and y help? And which way do we count the quadrants?

revise.summary: The axes split the plane into four quadrants numbered anticlockwise from the top right. The distance between two points comes from Pythagoras.
focus: Name the quadrant from the signs of x and y.
Know that points on axes are in no quadrant.
Find distances between points and from the origin.
remember: Distance = √[(x₂ − x₁)² + (y₂ − y₁)²].
Distance from origin = √(x² + y²).
traps: Don't number quadrants clockwise.
A point such as (0, −6) lies on an axis, not in a quadrant.
Don't add the changes; square, add, then take the square root.

learn.hook: A treasure map says: from the big banyan tree, walk 3 steps east and 4 steps north. Plotting points is exactly that!
points: To plot (a, b), start at the origin. Move a units along the x-axis: right if a is positive, left if a is negative.
From there move b units parallel to the y-axis: up if b is positive, down if b is negative. Mark the point.
Points with the same y-coordinate lie on one horizontal line; points with the same x-coordinate lie on one vertical line.
On graph paper choose a scale, for example 1 cm = 1 unit, and use it on both axes.
Length of a horizontal segment = difference of the x-coordinates; length of a vertical segment = difference of the y-coordinates.

example.q: Plot A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −1) and D(2, −1). What shape do they make, and what is its perimeter?
steps: AB is horizontal (same y): length = 2 − (−2) = 4 units
BC is vertical (same x): length = 3 − (−1) = 4 units
Similarly CD = 4 and DA = 4, and the sides meet at right angles
So ABCD is a square; perimeter = 4 × 4 = 16 units
example.answer: A square of side 4 units, perimeter 16 units

learn.reallife: Rangoli artists often mark dots on a grid first. Each dot is really a point with coordinates!

quiz.q: To plot (−4, 6), which move do you make first from the origin?
quiz.explain: The x-coordinate comes first. It is −4, so move 4 units to the left, then 6 units up.
steps: The x-coordinate comes first in (x, y).
x = −4 is negative, so move 4 units left first.
Then move 6 units up for y = 6.
quiz.mistake: Starts with the y-coordinate or ignores the negative sign

quiz.q: Which point lies on the same horizontal line as (3, −2)?
quiz.explain: A horizontal line keeps the y-coordinate the same. (−5, −2) has y = −2, just like (3, −2).
steps: Points on one horizontal line share the same y-coordinate.
quiz.mistake: Keeps the x-coordinate the same, which gives a vertical line

quiz.q: Kabir plots P(1, 2) and Q(1, 8). What is the length of PQ?
quiz.explain: P and Q have the same x-coordinate, so PQ is vertical. Its length is the difference of the y-coordinates.
steps: Same x, so PQ is vertical
quiz.mistake: Adds the y-coordinates instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Riya draws a rectangle with corners (0, 0), (6, 0), (6, 4) and (0, 4). What is its area?
quiz.explain: The length along the x-axis is 6 and the height along the y-axis is 4, so the area is 6 × 4.
quiz.mistake: Finds the perimeter (20) or adds the sides (10) instead of multiplying

quiz.q: Three corners of a square are (1, 1), (5, 1) and (5, 5). What is the fourth corner?
quiz.explain: The side from (1, 1) to (5, 1) has length 4. The missing corner is 4 units above (1, 1), at (1, 5).
quiz.mistake: Swaps x and y or continues the pattern in the wrong direction

quiz.q: Meena reads a point on a graph: it is 3 units below the x-axis and 7 units to the left of the y-axis. Which point is it?
quiz.explain: 7 units left of the y-axis gives x = −7; 3 units below the x-axis gives y = −3.
steps: 7 units left of the y-axis: x = −7.
quiz.mistake: Writes the numbers in the order they were read instead of (x, y)

quiz.q: On graph paper Joseph uses the scale 1 cm = 2 units. How far along the x-axis must he move to plot (10, 0)?
quiz.explain: Each centimetre stands for 2 units, so 10 units need 10 ÷ 2 = 5 cm.
quiz.mistake: Multiplies by the scale instead of dividing

quiz.q: Points A(−3, 2) and B(4, 2) are plotted. What is the length of AB?
quiz.explain: Same y-coordinate, so AB is horizontal. Length = 4 − (−3) = 7 units.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts 3 from 4 without handling the negative sign, getting 1

teach.ask: Gappu holds a pencil: "I want to put a dot at (−2, 5). Where do I even start?"
teach.praise: Start at the origin, go across first, then up or down. My dot landed perfectly!
teach.nudge: Which way do I go first, and does the minus sign change the direction?

revise.summary: To plot (a, b), start at the origin, move a units along the x-axis, then b units parallel to the y-axis. Same y means a horizontal line; same x means a vertical line.
focus: Plot points with negative coordinates.
Find lengths of horizontal and vertical segments.
Identify shapes from plotted points.
remember: Right if x > 0, left if x < 0; up if y > 0, down if y < 0.
Horizontal length = difference of x's; vertical length = difference of y's.
A(2, 3), B(−2, 3), C(−2, −1), D(2, −1): square of side 4, perimeter 16.
traps: Move along x first, not y.
Same x-coordinate gives a vertical line, not a horizontal one.
Subtracting a negative means adding: 2 − (−2) = 4.

learn.hook: Will Dadi's wheelchair fit through the door? Coordinates can answer before anyone tries!
points: Put one corner of a room at the origin with the walls along the axes; then every corner of every object gets coordinates.
Width of a door along a wall = difference of the coordinates of its two ends. Compare it with what must pass through, such as a wheelchair.
A hinged door sweeps a quarter circle whose radius is the door's width; furniture inside that sweep will be hit.
To place an object at the centre of a room, its centre is at (half the length, half the breadth); move half the object's sides each way to get its corners.
Plot given corners and look at the sides: four right angles and opposite sides equal means a rectangle; exactly one pair of parallel sides means a trapezium.

example.q: A room is 12 ft by 10 ft with a corner at O(0, 0). Place a 4 ft × 2 ft table at the centre. Give its corners.
steps: Half of 4 is 2 and half of 2 is 1
x from 6 − 2 = 4 to 6 + 2 = 8; y from 5 − 1 = 4 to 5 + 1 = 6

learn.reallife: Architects check door widths and furniture positions on coordinate plans before a house is built, so accessibility is planned, not patched.

A wheelchair 2.5 ft wide ___ pass a 3 ft door.
A door 3 ft wide swings through a quarter circle of radius ___ ft.

quiz.q: In a room plan, a door runs along the x-axis from (2, 0) to (5.5, 0), in feet. How wide is the door, in feet?
quiz.explain: Both ends are on the x-axis, so the width is the difference of the x-coordinates.
steps: Both ends are on the x-axis, so width = difference of x-coordinates.
quiz.mistake: Adds the coordinates instead of subtracting

quiz.q: A wheelchair needs at least 2.8 ft of clear width. A door goes from (4, 0) to (6.5, 0) in feet. Will the wheelchair pass?
options: Yes, the door is 10.5 ft wide
No, the door is only 2.5 ft wide
Yes, the door is 6.5 ft wide
No, the door is 4 ft wide
quiz.explain: Width = 6.5 − 4 = 2.5 ft, which is less than 2.8 ft.
steps: Answer: No, the door is only 2.5 ft wide
quiz.mistake: Reads one endpoint as the width

quiz.q: A 3 ft door is hinged at (0, 0) and swings into the room. A table leg is at (2, 2). Will the door hit it?
options: No, the leg is 4 ft from the hinge
No, doors only move along the wall
Yes, the leg is about 2.83 ft from the hinge, inside the 3 ft swing
quiz.explain: The door sweeps a quarter circle of radius 3. The leg's distance from the hinge is √(4 + 4) = √8 ≈ 2.83 ft, which is less than 3.
steps: 2.83 < 3, so the leg is inside the sweep
Answer: Yes, the leg is about 2.83 ft from the hinge, inside the 3 ft swing
quiz.mistake: Adds the coordinates instead of finding the straight distance

quiz.q: Kavya's room is 16 ft by 12 ft, with one corner at the origin. Where is the centre of the room?
quiz.explain: The centre is at half the length and half the breadth.
quiz.mistake: Swaps the order of the coordinates

quiz.q: A 6 ft × 4 ft carpet is centred at (8, 6). What is the x-coordinate of its left edge?
quiz.explain: Half of the 6 ft length is 3, so the left edge is 3 ft left of the centre.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts the full length instead of half of it

quiz.q: A wardrobe has corners (0, 2), (2, 2), (2, 8) and (0, 8) in feet. How much wall space along the y-axis does it use, in feet?
quiz.explain: Along the y-axis it runs from y = 2 to y = 8.
steps: The wardrobe runs along the y-axis from y = 2 to y = 8.
quiz.mistake: Takes the larger y-coordinate as the length

quiz.q: What shape do (0, 0), (8, 0), (6, 4) and (2, 4) make?
quiz.explain: The bottom (length 8) and top (length 4) are both horizontal, so they are parallel; the slanted sides are not parallel.
steps: Top side (2, 4) to (6, 4): horizontal, length 4. So top ∥ bottom.
Left side goes 2 right, 4 up; right side goes 2 left, 4 up: not parallel.
Exactly one pair of parallel sides makes a trapezium.
quiz.mistake: Thinks any four-sided figure with a horizontal base is a rectangle

quiz.q: The corners of a bathroom in a plan are (10, 0), (14, 0), (14, 5) and (10, 5). What is its floor area?
quiz.explain: It is a rectangle 4 ft by 5 ft.
quiz.mistake: Adds the sides instead of multiplying, or uses one coordinate as a side

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can coordinates tell if a door is wide enough or where the centre of a room is?"
teach.praise: Super! Subtract ends to get widths and halve sides to find the centre!
teach.nudge: How do you get the width from the two ends of a door? And how do you find the centre?

revise.summary: Put a room corner at the origin with walls on the axes, then every object gets coordinates. Use differences of coordinates for widths and half-lengths to centre objects.
focus: Find door and furniture widths from coordinates.
Place an object at the centre of a room.
Identify rectangles and trapeziums from corners.
remember: Width along a wall = difference of the coordinates of the ends.
Centre of an L × B room = (L/2, B/2).
A door sweeps a quarter circle of radius = door width.
traps: Don't add coordinates to find a width.
Move half the object's side each way, not the full side.
A four-sided shape with a horizontal base is not always a rectangle.

topics.title: Triangles, right angles and reflections on the grid

learn.hook: Fold your graph paper along the y-axis: every point lands on its mirror twin!
points: To find the sides of a triangle from its corners, apply the distance formula to each pair of vertices.
A side is parallel to the x-axis if its ends share the same y-coordinate, and parallel to the y-axis if they share the same x-coordinate. A horizontal and a vertical side are perpendicular.
A quick right triangle: pick corners like (a, b), (c, b), (a, d). The legs are |c − a| and |d − b|, and the hypotenuse comes from Pythagoras.
Reflecting in the y-axis turns (x, y) into (−x, y); reflecting in the x-axis turns (x, y) into (x, −y).
A reflection is a flip, not a stretch: all side lengths and angles of the figure stay the same.

example.q: Find the sides of the triangle A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 5). Is it right-angled?
steps: AB is horizontal and AC vertical, so angle A = 90°

learn.reallife: Rangoli artists use mirror symmetry: a design reflected across a line keeps all its sizes.

games.title: Grid facts
items: Reflecting a triangle in the y-axis can change its side lengths.
A reflection keeps every length the same.
The side from (2, 3) to (7, 3) is parallel to the x-axis.
Both ends have y = 3, so it is horizontal.
The side from (2, 3) to (2, 9) is parallel to the x-axis.
Same x-coordinate means it is vertical, parallel to the y-axis.
A horizontal side and a vertical side meet at a right angle.
The axes are perpendicular, so lines parallel to them are too.
The mirror image of (4, −1) in the x-axis is (4, 1).
Only the sign of y changes.

quiz.q: Find the length of side PQ of triangle P(−2, 1), Q(4, 9), R(4, 1).
quiz.explain: Across 6 and up 8, so PQ is the hypotenuse of a 6-8 right triangle.
quiz.mistake: Adds the horizontal and vertical changes

quiz.q: In triangle P(−2, 1), Q(4, 9), R(4, 1), which side is parallel to the y-axis?
quiz.explain: Q and R both have x = 4, so QR is vertical, parallel to the y-axis.
steps: A side is parallel to the y-axis if its ends share the same x-coordinate.
Q(4, 9) and R(4, 1) both have x = 4.
PR has the same y (1), so it is parallel to the x-axis.
quiz.mistake: Mixes up parallel to the x-axis with parallel to the y-axis

quiz.q: What is the mirror image of (−5, 3) in the y-axis?
quiz.explain: Reflecting in the y-axis changes only the sign of the x-coordinate.
steps: Reflecting in the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y).
quiz.mistake: Changes the sign of the wrong coordinate

quiz.q: A triangle with sides 5, 6 and 7 units is reflected in the x-axis. What is the length of the longest side of the image?
quiz.explain: A reflection does not change any length.
steps: A reflection is a flip, not a stretch.
All side lengths stay the same.
Longest side stays 7 units. Lengths are never negative.
quiz.mistake: Thinks reflecting makes lengths negative

quiz.q: Neha wants a right triangle with legs 5 and 12 using the corner (0, 0). Which pair of other corners works?
quiz.explain: (5, 0) is on the x-axis and (0, 12) on the y-axis, giving legs 5 and 12 meeting at a right angle at the origin.
steps: Legs must be along perpendicular lines through (0, 0).
(5, 0) is 5 units along the x-axis; (0, 12) is 12 units up the y-axis.
These legs meet at a right angle at the origin.
quiz.mistake: Picks points that are not on perpendicular lines through the corner

quiz.q: What is the hypotenuse of the right triangle with corners (0, 0), (5, 0) and (0, 12)?
quiz.explain: Use Pythagoras on the legs 5 and 12.
quiz.mistake: Forgets to take the square root

quiz.q: Triangle A(1, 2), B(6, 2), C(1, 7). At which vertex is the right angle?
quiz.explain: AB is horizontal (same y) and AC is vertical (same x). They meet at A.
steps: AB: A(1, 2), B(6, 2) have the same y, so AB is horizontal.
AC: A(1, 2), C(1, 7) have the same x, so AC is vertical.
Horizontal and vertical sides meet at A at 90°.
quiz.mistake: Assumes the right angle is always at the last listed vertex

quiz.q: The point (2, −6) is reflected in the y-axis and then in the x-axis. Where does it end up?
quiz.explain: First (2, −6) → (−2, −6), then (−2, −6) → (−2, 6). Both signs change.
quiz.mistake: Applies only one of the two reflections

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the sides of a triangle from its corners, and what happens when I reflect it?"
teach.praise: Perfect! Distance formula for sides, sign flip for reflections, and lengths stay the same!
teach.nudge: Which formula gives each side? And does a reflection change the lengths?

revise.summary: Use the distance formula for the sides of a triangle on the grid. A horizontal and a vertical side meet at a right angle. Reflections change signs but not lengths.
focus: Find side lengths from vertices.
Spot the right angle using horizontal and vertical sides.
Reflect points in the axes.
remember: Same y → parallel to the x-axis; same x → parallel to the y-axis.
Reflect in the y-axis: (x, y) → (−x, y). In the x-axis: (x, y) → (x, −y).
A(1, 1), B(4, 1), C(1, 5): sides 3, 4, 5, right angle at A.
traps: Don't change the sign of the wrong coordinate.
Reflection never makes a length negative.
The right angle is where the horizontal and vertical sides meet, not always the last vertex.

topics.title: Lines parallel to axes and collinear points

learn.hook: Three friends standing in a perfectly straight queue: can coordinates prove it?
points: All points on a line parallel to the y-axis share the same x-coordinate, so you can predict the next point's coordinates and quadrant from the sign pattern.
A horizontal line y = 3 passes through Quadrants II and I; a vertical line x = −4 passes through Quadrants II and III.
Three points A, B, C are collinear (on one straight line) when the longest distance equals the sum of the other two: AB + BC = AC.
If the sum is bigger than the longest distance, the points form a triangle instead.
With only positive numbers, the origin must sit at a corner and nothing can be placed to its left or below; negatives let the origin be anywhere, such as the centre.

example.q: Are A(1, 1), B(4, 5) and C(7, 9) collinear?

learn.reallife: Surveyors laying a straight water pipeline check that marker posts are collinear before digging.

items.text: The line x = −2 crosses Quadrants II and ___.
If AB = 4, BC = 6, AC = 10, then A, B, C are ___.
Without negative numbers the origin must be at a ___ of the grid.

quiz.q: Points (−5, 2), (−5, 1), (−5, 0), (−5, −1) go down a line. In which quadrant is the next point (−5, −2)?
quiz.explain: x stays −5 (negative) and y is now −2 (negative): (−, −) is Quadrant III.
steps: The line keeps x = −5, which is negative.
quiz.mistake: Forgets the y-coordinate has become negative

quiz.q: Which point lies on the same vertical line as (6, −3)?
quiz.explain: A vertical line keeps the x-coordinate fixed. Only (6, 10) has x = 6.
steps: A vertical line keeps the x-coordinate fixed.
quiz.mistake: Thinks a vertical line keeps y fixed

quiz.q: The line y = −4 is drawn. Which quadrants does it pass through?
quiz.explain: y = −4 is a horizontal line below the x-axis, running through the bottom-left and bottom-right quadrants.
steps: y = −4 is a horizontal line 4 units below the x-axis.
It runs through left (x < 0) and right (x > 0) with y negative.
quiz.mistake: Confuses horizontal and vertical lines

quiz.q: For points A, B, C, AB = 7, BC = 5 and AC = 12. What can you say?
options: A, B and C are collinear
quiz.explain: AB + BC = 7 + 5 = 12 = AC, so B lies on the segment AC.
steps: Answer: A, B and C are collinear
quiz.mistake: Thinks any three points always form a triangle

quiz.q: Are P(0, 0), Q(3, 4) and R(9, 12) collinear? Use distances.
steps: Answer: Yes, because PQ + QR = PR = 15
quiz.mistake: Compares only two of the three distances

quiz.q: Points A(0, 0), B(4, 3) and C(4, 0). AB = 5, BC = 3, AC = 4. Are they collinear?
options: No, 3 + 4 = 7 is more than the longest side 5
No, because they are all positive
quiz.explain: For collinear points the two shorter distances must add to exactly the longest. Here 3 + 4 = 7 ≠ 5, so they form a triangle.
steps: Collinear means the two shorter distances add up to the longest.
Longest is AB = 5. Others: BC + AC = 3 + 4 = 7.
7 ≠ 5, so A, B, C form a triangle.
Answer: No, 3 + 4 = 7 is more than the longest side 5
quiz.mistake: Adds the wrong pair of distances

quiz.q: Rohit draws a grid with no negative numbers to map his school. What must he do?
options: Put the origin at the centre
Put the origin at a corner so everything is to its right and above
quiz.explain: Without negatives, nothing can lie left of or below the origin, so it must be at the bottom-left corner.
steps: Without negatives, nothing can be left of or below the origin.
So the origin must be at the bottom-left corner.
Answer: Put the origin at a corner so everything is to its right and above
quiz.mistake: Thinks negatives make no difference to where the origin can go

quiz.q: What is a limitation of a coordinate system without negative numbers?
options: Distances cannot be found at all
Only two points can be plotted
Places left of or below the origin cannot be named
quiz.explain: Negative coordinates are needed for points on the other side of each axis.
steps: Points left of or below the origin need negative coordinates.
Without negatives, they cannot be named.
Distances can still be found and axes can still be perpendicular.
Answer: Places left of or below the origin cannot be named
quiz.mistake: Thinks distances depend on having negative numbers

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How can I tell if three points lie on one straight line?"
teach.praise: Spot on! Two shorter distances adding up to the longest means one straight line!
teach.nudge: Which distances do you compare? What must the two smaller ones add up to?

revise.summary: Points on a line parallel to an axis share one coordinate. Three points are collinear when the two shorter distances add up exactly to the longest.
focus: Predict points and quadrants on lines parallel to axes.
Say which quadrants a line like y = −4 passes through.
Test collinearity with distances.
remember: Vertical line: x fixed. Horizontal line: y fixed.
Collinear: AB + BC = AC (AC longest).
Without negatives, the origin must be at a corner.
traps: A vertical line keeps x fixed, not y.
If the shorter two add to more than the longest, the points form a triangle.
Compare all three distances, not just two.

topics.title: Circles, squares and grids in action

learn.hook: A game designer must know whether two circles on a screen touch. Coordinates make the call!
points: A point (x, y) is inside a circle of radius r centred at the origin if x² + y² < r², on it if x² + y² = r², and outside if x² + y² > r².
Two circles cut each other when the distance between centres is less than the sum of the radii (and more than their difference); they just touch when it equals the sum.
A circle fits inside a screen if its centre is at least r away from every edge.
Four points form a square when all four sides are equal and both diagonals are equal. Area = side².

In a city grid, each street intersection can be named by an ordered pair (street number, avenue number). An isosceles triangle can be planned by placing the apex on the perpendicular bisector of the base.

example.q: Does A(1, 1), B(4, 2), C(3, 5), D(0, 4) form a square? Find its area.
steps: All sides equal and diagonals equal: a square

learn.reallife: Mobile games check collisions between round objects by comparing the distance between centres with the sum of the radii.

games.title: Circle of radius 5 at the origin
Squares and circles
items: Four equal sides always make a square.
A rhombus also has four equal sides; diagonals must be equal too.
Circles with centres 10 apart and radii 4 and 5 do not meet.
4 + 5 = 9 is less than 10.
Circles with centres 6 apart and radii 4 and 5 intersect.
6 is less than 9 and more than 5 − 4 = 1.
A square with side √8 has area 8.
Area = side² = 8.
(0, 0), (2, 0), (0, 2) can be corners of an isosceles right triangle.
Two legs of length 2 meet at a right angle at the origin.

quiz.q: Is the point (5, 12) inside, on or outside the circle of radius 13 centred at the origin?
quiz.mistake: Adds the coordinates (17) and compares with 13

quiz.q: Where is (−6, 7) compared with the circle x² + y² = 81 (radius 9)?
quiz.explain: 36 + 49 = 85, which is more than 81.
quiz.mistake: Ignores the minus sign wrongly, or compares with 9 instead of 81

quiz.q: A screen is 100 pixels wide and 60 tall, with corners (0, 0) and (100, 60). Does a circle of radius 35 centred at (50, 30) fit?
options: No, it pokes out only at the sides
No, it pokes out at the top and bottom
Yes, it just touches the sides
quiz.explain: The centre is only 30 from the top and bottom edges, which is less than the radius 35. It is 50 from the side edges, so the sides are fine.
steps: Answer: No, it pokes out at the top and bottom
quiz.mistake: Checks only the width of the screen

quiz.q: Two circles have centres (0, 0) and (6, 8), with radii 4 and 5. Do they meet?
options: Yes, they cross at two points
One circle is inside the other
No, the centres are 10 apart and 4 + 5 = 9
quiz.explain: Distance between centres = √(36 + 64) = 10, which is more than the sum of radii 9.
steps: Answer: No, the centres are 10 apart and 4 + 5 = 9
quiz.mistake: Compares the radii with a single coordinate instead of the distance

quiz.q: Show that P(0, 0), Q(3, 0), R(3, 3), S(0, 3) is a square. What is its area?
quiz.explain: All four sides are 3 and both diagonals are √18, so it is a square of side 3.
quiz.mistake: Gives the perimeter instead of the area

quiz.q: Points (0, 0), (2, 1), (1, 3), (−1, 2): each side is √5 and both diagonals are √10. What is the area of this square?
quiz.explain: Area of a square = side² = (√5)² = 5.
quiz.mistake: Squares the diagonal instead of the side

quiz.q: In a city grid, Shreya is at the corner of Street 3 and Avenue 5, written (3, 5). She walks 4 streets east and 2 avenues south. Where is she?
quiz.explain: East increases the street number by 4; south decreases the avenue number by 2.
quiz.mistake: Moves the wrong coordinate for each direction

quiz.q: A triangle has base A(−3, 0), B(3, 0). Which third vertex makes the two slanting sides equal (an isosceles triangle)?
quiz.explain: A point on the y-axis is equally far from (−3, 0) and (3, 0), so the two sides from the apex are equal.
steps: The apex must be equally far from A(−3, 0) and B(3, 0).
Such points lie on the perpendicular bisector of AB, the y-axis (x = 0).
Only (0, 5) has x = 0. Each slant side = √(9 + 25) = √34.
quiz.mistake: Chooses a vertex directly above one end of the base

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I know if a point is inside a circle around the origin?"
teach.praise: Brilliant! Compare x² + y² with r squared!
teach.nudge: What do you calculate from x and y? And what do you compare it with?

revise.summary: Coordinates help test points against circles, check squares, fit shapes on screens and name street corners. Compare x² + y² with r² for a circle centred at the origin.
focus: Decide if a point is inside, on or outside a circle.
Test if four points form a square and find its area.
Place an apex for an isosceles triangle.
remember: Inside: x² + y² < r²; on: = r²; outside: > r².
Two circles cut if distance between centres < sum of radii (and > difference).
Square: four equal sides and equal diagonals; area = side².
Apex on the perpendicular bisector of the base gives equal slant sides.
traps: Don't add coordinates; square them.
Area of a square is side², not diagonal².
Checking only the screen width is not enough.

learn.hook: Two friends live at different corners of the city. Where should they meet so that both walk equally?
points: The midpoint of A(x₁, y₁) and B(x₂, y₂) is ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2): average the x's and average the y's.
To check if M is the midpoint, compute the midpoint formula and see if it gives M.
If M is the midpoint and A is one end, the other end is B = (2 × M's x − A's x, 2 × M's y − A's y).
Points of trisection divide AB into three equal parts: each step is one-third of the change in x and y, so the points are A + (1/3)(B − A) and A + (2/3)(B − A).
If the midpoints of the sides of a triangle are known, the vertices can be found by solving: each vertex equals (sum of the two midpoints next to it) minus the opposite midpoint.

example.q: Find the points of trisection of A(1, 2) and B(7, 11).
steps: Change in x = 6, change in y = 9

learn.reallife: A delivery app can suggest a fair meeting point halfway between two friends' homes using the midpoint formula.

items.q: Midpoint x = 5, one end x = 2. Other end x?
Midpoint y = 0, one end y = 6. Other end y?
Midpoint x = −1, one end x = 3. Other end x?

quiz.q: What is the midpoint of A(−4, 6) and B(8, 2)?
quiz.explain: Average the x-coordinates and average the y-coordinates.
quiz.mistake: Subtracts instead of adding before halving

quiz.q: Is M(3, 5) the midpoint of P(1, 2) and Q(5, 9)?
quiz.mistake: Checks only the x-coordinate

quiz.q: M(2, −1) is the midpoint of AB and A is (−3, 4). What is the x-coordinate of B?
steps: B's x = 2 × M's x − A's x
quiz.mistake: Halves instead of doubling, or forgets the minus sign

quiz.q: M(2, −1) is the midpoint of AB and A is (−3, 4). What is the y-coordinate of B?
steps: B's y = 2 × M's y − A's y
quiz.mistake: Adds A's y instead of subtracting

quiz.q: Which point divides the segment from (0, 0) to (12, 6) at one-third of the way from the origin?
quiz.explain: One-third of the way means one-third of each change: 12/3 = 4 and 6/3 = 2.
quiz.mistake: Takes the midpoint instead of the trisection point

quiz.q: Find the second point of trisection (two-thirds of the way) from A(−3, 1) to B(6, 7).
quiz.explain: The change is 9 in x and 6 in y; two-thirds of that is 6 and 4. Add to A.
quiz.mistake: Stops at the first trisection point

quiz.q: The midpoints of the sides of a triangle are D(3, 4), E(5, 2) and F(1, 1). The vertex between midpoints D and E (opposite F) is D + E − F. What is it?
quiz.mistake: Averages the midpoints instead of adding and subtracting

quiz.q: Gurpreet's home is at (−2, 8) and Asha's at (6, 0). Where is the halfway meeting point?
quiz.mistake: Uses the difference of the coordinates instead of the sum

teach.ask: Gappu asks: "How do I find the point exactly halfway between two points?"
teach.praise: Excellent! Add and halve the x's, add and halve the y's!
teach.nudge: What do you do with the two x-coordinates? And the two y-coordinates?

revise.summary: The midpoint of two points averages their x's and y's. Points of trisection are one-third and two-thirds of the way from A to B.
focus: Find and check midpoints.
Find the other end of a segment from a midpoint.
Find points of trisection.
remember: Midpoint = ((x₁ + x₂)/2, (y₁ + y₂)/2).
Other end B = (2 × M's x − A's x, 2 × M's y − A's y).
Trisection: A + (1/3)(B − A) and A + (2/3)(B − A).
traps: Add the coordinates before halving; don't subtract.
Don't stop at the first trisection point.
Check both coordinates when testing a midpoint.
